scenes.tts: If one input depolarizes a cell, do two identical inputs depolarize it twice as much?
scenes.visual: Two identical red ropes side by side, with a question: 2 inputs = 2 × the depolarization?
scenes.narration: If one input depolarizes a cell, do two identical inputs depolarize it twice as much?

scenes.tts: Take our cell. The leak is ten nanosiemens, tied at minus 65 millivolts. Threshold is minus 50.
scenes.caption: Take our cell. The leak is 10 nS, tied at −65 mV. Threshold is −50 mV.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale with the grey leak rope at −65 mV and a dashed threshold line at −50 mV. Label: illustrative cell, C = 200 pF.
scenes.narration: Take our cell. The leak is 10 nS, tied at −65 mV. Threshold is −50 mV.

scenes.tts: All the values here are illustrative. The cell is passive, and its voltage is the same everywhere. Voltages above threshold are passive predictions, with the spike switched off.
scenes.visual: Small print card: illustrative values; isopotential, passive cell; values above −50 mV are passive predictions (spike mechanism switched off); real thresholds shift with channel state.
scenes.narration: All the values here are illustrative. The cell is passive, and its voltage is the same everywhere. Voltages above threshold are passive predictions, with the spike switched off.

scenes.tts: Open a steady excitatory input of five nanosiemens, tied at zero millivolts.
scenes.caption: Open a steady excitatory input of 5 nS, tied at 0 mV.
scenes.visual: A red AMPA rope, 5 nS, appears, tied at 0 mV.
scenes.narration: Open a steady excitatory input of 5 nS, tied at 0 mV.

scenes.tts: The passive prediction is near minus 43 millivolts. That is about 22 millivolts of depolarization, above threshold. A real cell with this threshold would fire on the way.
scenes.caption: The passive prediction is near −43 mV. That is about 22 mV of depolarization, above threshold. A real cell with this threshold would fire on the way.
scenes.visual: A dashed ghost marker labelled 'passive prediction' slides to −43.3 mV, past the dashed threshold line; a spark marks where a real cell would fire at −50 mV. On screen only: (10 × −65 + 5 × 0)/15 = −43.3 mV; depolarization 21.7 mV.
scenes.narration: The passive prediction is near −43 mV. That is about 22 mV of depolarization, above threshold. A real cell with this threshold would fire on the way.

scenes.tts: It gets there with a shorter time constant, about 13 milliseconds, because the total conductance grew.
scenes.caption: It gets there with a shorter time constant, about 13 ms, because the total conductance grew.
scenes.visual: On screen only: τ_eff = 200 pF / 15 nS = 13.3 ms.
scenes.narration: It gets there with a shorter time constant, about 13 ms, because the total conductance grew.

scenes.tts: Now open a second, identical input at the same time. Does the depolarization double, to about 43 millivolts?
scenes.caption: Now open a second, identical input at the same time. Does the depolarization double, to about 43 mV?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. A second 5 nS rope. Does the depolarization double to about 43 mV? A ghost marker waits at −21.7 mV, labelled 'if it doubled'.
scenes.narration: Now open a second, identical input at the same time. Does the depolarization double, to about 43 mV?

scenes.tts: No. The passive prediction is about minus 32 and a half millivolts. That is about one and a half times as much, not twice.
scenes.caption: No. The passive prediction is about −32.5 mV. That is about one and a half times as much, not twice.
scenes.visual: The dashed passive-prediction marker stops at −32.5 mV, well short of the ghost at −21.7 mV. A bar pair: expected 43.3 mV, got 32.5 mV.
scenes.narration: No. The passive prediction is about −32.5 mV. That is about one and a half times as much, not twice.

scenes.tts: To see why, measure the voltage from rest. Then the leak drops out of the average.
scenes.visual: On screen: V_ss − EL = (gE × (EE − EL) + gI × (EI − EL)) / (gL + gE + gI). The leak's term fades out.
scenes.narration: To see why, measure the voltage from rest. Then the leak drops out of the average.

scenes.tts: The leak is tied at rest, so its top-line term is zero. But the leak is still in the bottom line, and still carries current.
scenes.visual: The grey leak rope's top-line term reads 10 × 0 = 0 and fades from the top line only; the leak stays in the bottom line and its rope stays on the scale. The red rope's term remains.
scenes.narration: The leak is tied at rest, so its top-line term is zero. But the leak is still in the bottom line, and still carries current.

scenes.tts: Each top-line term is a synapse's conductance, times how far its rope's end sits from rest.
scenes.visual: The top line glows. Under it: g × (E − EL), the pull that rope would have with the marker at rest.
scenes.narration: Each top-line term is a synapse's conductance, times how far its rope's end sits from rest.

scenes.tts: The bottom line is still the total conductance.
scenes.visual: The bottom line glows: total conductance.
scenes.narration: The bottom line is still the total conductance.

scenes.tts: Two inputs double the top line. But they also enlarge the bottom line.
scenes.visual: Side by side, held on screen through the next two scenes: one input 325 / 15 = 21.7 mV; two inputs 650 / 20 = 32.5 mV. The top line doubles; the bottom line grows from 15 to 20.
scenes.narration: Two inputs double the top line. But they also enlarge the bottom line.

scenes.tts: With one input, the top is 325, over 15. With two, the top doubles to 650, but the bottom also grows, to 20.
scenes.visual: The two fractions stay on screen: 5 × 65 over 10 + 5, and 10 × 65 over 10 + 10. The doubled top glows; the bottom's change from 15 to 20 is circled.
scenes.narration: With one input, the top is 325, over 15. With two, the top doubles to 650, but the bottom also grows, to 20.

scenes.tts: So the second input dilutes the first.
scenes.visual: Both red ropes stay equally thick. A share bar shows the first rope's share of total conductance shrinking as the second appears.
scenes.narration: So the second input dilutes the first.

scenes.tts: That is the same effect, seen as ropes. The marker is nearer zero millivolts, so each ampa rope's driving force has shrunk.
scenes.caption: That is the same effect, seen as ropes. The marker is nearer 0 mV, so each AMPA rope's driving force has shrunk.
scenes.visual: Driving-force arrows on the two red ropes shorten as the marker moves toward 0 mV.
scenes.narration: That is the same effect, seen as ropes. The marker is nearer 0 mV, so each AMPA rope's driving force has shrunk.

scenes.tts: This is sublinear summation. Inputs sharing one small patch of membrane show it most.
scenes.visual: Label: sublinear summation. Two synapses drawn close together on one small patch of membrane.
scenes.narration: This is sublinear summation. Inputs sharing one small patch of membrane show it most.

scenes.tts: Notice where the surprise lived: in the bottom line, the total conductance.
scenes.visual: The bottom line of the formula is circled.
scenes.narration: Notice where the surprise lived: in the bottom line, the total conductance.

scenes.tts: Each new input adds to the total conductance. So the voltage settles at a weighted average, not a sum of millivolts. Small inputs nearly add. Large ones fall short.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: conductances add; millivolts add only approximately, less so for large inputs. Two strong inputs gave one and a half times, not twice.
scenes.narration: Each new input adds to the total conductance. So the voltage settles at a weighted average, not a sum of millivolts. Small inputs nearly add. Large ones fall short.
